standard.title: Create Descriptions, Explanations and Arguments
standard.description: create descriptions, explanations and arguments, using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms that incorporate and acknowledge research findings
standard.prior_knowledge: From Y8 AC9HE8S05 (direct predecessor): create descriptions and explanations using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms, referencing information and data from sources. Students can create descriptions and explanations with source references. Y9 adds two moves: (1) arguments — a new text type requiring a reasoned position with evidence; and (2) acknowledge research findings — moving from referencing to formal acknowledgement of sources. Y9 also adds audience orientation and appropriate tone.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and arguments, using economic and business knowledge, concepts and terms that incorporate and acknowledge research findings.

nodes.label: Orientating the audience using concepts and terms
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop responses that orient the audience to an economic or business issue using relevant concepts and terms.
nodes.minimum_width: Write an opening section for an economic or business response that orients a specified audience to the issue using at least two relevant economic or business terms or concepts.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a response to an issue that orients the audience (peers or business representatives) using relevant economic and business terms and concepts from the elaboration list: interdependence, trade, comparative advantage, competitive advantage, globalisation, supply chain, financial risks and rewards, return on investment, debt, savings buffer, scams, financial landscape, corporate social responsibility, financial planning, insurance. The orientation should establish what the issue is, why it matters to the audience, and the key concepts that frame the analysis.
wider: Write audience-oriented openings for the same economic issue for two different audiences (e.g. peers and business representatives) — demonstrating how vocabulary, assumed knowledge and framing shift between audiences
Evaluate a provided economic response opening and revise it to better orient a specific audience — explaining each revision decision
Write an orientation to a First Nations economic issue that appropriately contextualises the issue for a non-specialist audience without oversimplifying or appropriating
nodes.hinge_reason: Audience orientation determines whether the subsequent explanation and argument are accessible to the reader. A response that fails to orient the audience creates a comprehension gap that undermines the force of the argument regardless of its technical accuracy.

response_modes.reason: Effective orientation requires three decisions: who is the audience, what do they already know, and what do they need to be told to follow what comes next. Making these decisions explicit before drafting prevents students from writing only for themselves.

success_criteria: Identifies the target audience explicitly or through audience-appropriate vocabulary choices
Uses at least two relevant economic or business terms or concepts in the orientation
The orientation establishes what the issue is and why it matters to the specified audience

nodes.label: Explaining and supporting decisions with data representations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain decisions and conclusions related to an economic or business issue, supported by visual displays or data representations, and acknowledge research sources.
nodes.minimum_width: Write an explanation of one conclusion from an economic investigation, supported by one data representation (table, graph or graphic organiser), and acknowledge the source.
nodes.typical_width: Explain decisions and conclusions related to an economic or business issue supported by representations of relevant data — applying the elaboration examples (visual displays, graphic organisers, tables and graphs, explanations, procedures or reports). Acknowledge research findings formally. The explanation should: state the conclusion, show how the data representation supports it, explain the reasoning connecting data to conclusion, and cite the source.
wider: Construct a multi-representation explanation — using a combination of text, table, and graph to build an explanation that uses each representation for what it does best
Evaluate the data representations used in a published economic report and explain which are well-chosen for the conclusions they support and which are misleading or poorly matched

Apply formal acknowledgement conventions to a range of source types (government statistics, news articles, expert reports) and explain why proper acknowledgement matters for the credibility of economic arguments

response_modes.reason: Data-supported explanation requires repeated practice to build the habit of connecting the representation to the conclusion explicitly rather than inserting it as decoration. Students commonly include graphs without explaining what they show or why they support the claim.

success_criteria: Supports at least one conclusion with a data representation (table, graph, or graphic organiser)
Explains what the representation shows and how it supports the conclusion
Acknowledges at least one research source

nodes.label: Constructing reasoned arguments with appropriate tone
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can present a reasoned argument in relation to an economic or business issue, applying tone appropriate to the purpose and audience.
nodes.minimum_width: Write one reasoned argument on an economic or business issue — stating a position, providing at least one evidence-based reason, and using a tone appropriate to a specified audience.
nodes.typical_width: Present a reasoned argument in relation to an economic or business issue applying tone appropriate to purpose — using the elaboration example (authoritative tone when explaining trends in data to peers or business representatives). The argument should: state a clear position on the issue; provide evidence-based reasons that support the position; address the issue's complexity; apply an authoritative, substantiated tone (not casual, not assertive without evidence); and acknowledge research findings. Distinguish an argument from an explanation — an argument stakes a position; an explanation describes how something works.
wider: Write arguments from competing stakeholder positions on the same economic issue (e.g. free trade vs protectionism from an industry perspective vs a consumer perspective) — demonstrating how evidence selection and framing differ by position
Evaluate two arguments on the same economic issue for reasoning quality — identifying which makes stronger use of evidence, more valid causal reasoning, and more appropriate tone
Write an argument that explicitly anticipates and addresses a counter-argument — explaining why acknowledging the counter-argument strengthens rather than weakens the overall argument

response_modes.reason: The argument structure (position → reason → evidence → explanation of how evidence supports reason) is new at Y9 and must be made explicit. Students commonly produce explanations that state conclusions without staking a position, or staking positions without evidence — neither is an argument.

Arguments in Economics and Business vary in tone and evidence demands across contexts (academic, business, policy, consumer). Practising across contexts — not just in one academic format — builds tone flexibility and evidence-selection judgment.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Writing arguments from competing stakeholder positions, evaluating argument quality, and addressing counter-arguments build sophisticated rhetorical and evidential reasoning skills that transfer across disciplines and to civic discourse.
success_criteria: States a clear position on the economic or business issue
Provides at least one evidence-based reason that supports the position
Applies a tone appropriate to the specified audience and purpose
